```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# The searches below call OpenAlex and spend credits, so like the live tests
# they only run when SCYTHE_TEST_OPENALEX=true, and never on CI. Otherwise the
# vignette shows the code without running it, which keeps R CMD check offline
# and free.
live <- isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv("SCYTHE_TEST_OPENALEX", "false"))) &&
  !isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv("CI", "false")))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = live)
```

This vignette uses `citation_search_openalex()` to find articles that cite
datasets in the [Arctic Data Center](https://arcticdata.io) (ADC), whose DOIs
all start with `10.18739`. It works through the search in stages, from
cheapest to most expensive, so that each stage checks the one before it
before you spend more of your OpenAlex budget.

## How OpenAlex charges for searches

OpenAlex charges credits for each request against a daily budget: 1,000
credits a day without an API key, and more with one (typically 10,000 credits a day). 
`citation_search_openalex()` has two search methods, and their costs are very different:

- **`"graph"`** follows OpenAlex's citation graph, finding works whose
  reference lists resolve to the dataset. It costs about 3 credits per batch
  of 100 DOIs, so even the whole ADC costs a few hundred credits. The graph 
  search examines the citation relationships that OpenAlex has already resolved, 
  so it only finds citations that are already in the citation graph, but it is inexpensive.
- **`"text"`** runs an exact full-text search for each DOI, which also finds
  DOIs mentioned outside reference lists, for example in data availability
  statements. Screening costs 10 credits per batch of 100 DOIs, but each DOI
  that matches costs about `20 * log2(batch size)` more credits to work out
  which DOI in the batch matched. The cost is driven by how many datasets are
  cited, not how many are searched.

Before sending any request, `citation_search_openalex()` estimates the cost
and stops if it exceeds `max_credits`. Setting `max_credits = 0` therefore
gives a free estimate: the function prints the estimate and stops without
sending anything. Each stage below starts with one.

## Setup

Every search writes its review logs and checkpoints to `work_dir`. A
checkpoint records each completed batch, so rerunning a stage, on the same
day or later, skips the batches already done. Keep `batch_size` and `since`
the same between runs, or the checkpoints won't match.

```{r work-dir, eval = TRUE}
library(scythe)

work_dir <- if (live) path.expand("~/scythe-adc") else tempfile("scythe-adc")
dir.create(work_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
options(scythe.log_dir = work_dir)

show_status <- function(res) str(attr(res, "openalex_status")[
  c("complete", "stopped", "paused_until", "estimate", "credits_used", "requests")])
```

Set an OpenAlex API key for a larger daily budget, and a contact email to send
with each request. This only needs doing once, since the keys are kept in your
operating system's credential store.

```{r keys, eval = FALSE}
scythe_set_key("openalex", "<your key>")
# Or use `scythe_set_key("openalex_mailto", "<you@example.org>")`
```

You can check whether a key is set with:
```{r key-check, eval = FALSE}
!is.na(scythe_get_key("openalex"))   # TRUE means a key is set
```

## Stage 1: Known citations

The first stage searches for a few ADC citations already recorded in the
package's test data, to check that the search works end to end before
spending more. The test data lists citations found by several services, so
the `sources` column records which ones previously found each citation. Where a dataset
is cited in a form that isn't a DOI, such as a catalog URL, its `dataone_pid`
is used instead.

```{r known, eval = TRUE}
known <- read.csv(system.file("testdata", "test-citations.csv", package = "scythe"))
known$dataset_doi <- scythe:::normalize_doi(known$dataset_id_as_cited)
known$dataset_doi <- ifelse(is.na(known$dataset_doi),
                            scythe:::normalize_doi(known$dataone_pid), known$dataset_doi)
known <- known[grepl("^10\\.18739/", known$dataset_doi), ]
known <- aggregate(source ~ pub_id + dataset_doi, known,
                   function(x) paste(sort(unique(x)), collapse = ", "))
names(known)[names(known) == "source"] <- "sources"
known
```

Estimate the cost, then run both methods on these datasets:

```{r known-search}
try(citation_search_openalex(unique(known$dataset_doi), max_credits = 0))

positives <- citation_search_openalex(unique(known$dataset_doi),
                                      checkpoint_dir = work_dir, max_credits = 200)
show_status(positives)
```

Then check which known citations were found:

```{r known-check}
pair <- function(article, dataset) {
  paste(scythe:::normalize_doi(article), scythe:::normalize_doi(dataset))
}
known$found <- pair(known$pub_id, known$dataset_doi) %in%
  pair(positives$article_id, positives$dataset_id)
known
```

A citation that OpenAlex found before (`sources` includes `openalex`) should
be found again, so `FALSE` on one of those rows is a bug. `FALSE` on a row
found only by other services is a gap in OpenAlex's coverage instead. For
example, Radville et al. (2016) cites `10.18739/A23H1N` in its text, and
Springer's API finds it there. But that text is missing from OpenAlex's
full-text index, and the paper's reference list doesn't include the dataset,
so neither method can find it. These rows show what OpenAlex misses compared
with the other services.

Any matches that aren't in the test data are new, and worth checking by hand:

```{r known-new}
positives[!pair(positives$article_id, positives$dataset_id) %in%
            pair(known$pub_id, known$dataset_doi), ]
```

## Stage 2: All current ADC DOIs

The second stage collects the DOIs to search: every current ADC metadata
record in the [DataONE](https://www.dataone.org) search index, leaving out
versions that have been replaced by newer ones. There were about 6,000 in
October 2026. Saving the list keeps later runs searching the same DOIs, in
the same order, so that their checkpoints match.

```{r adc-dois}
solr <- paste0("https://cn.dataone.org/cn/v2/query/solr/",
               "?q=id:doi%5C:10.18739*+AND+formatType:METADATA+AND+-obsoletedBy:*",
               "&fl=id&rows=20000&wt=csv")
adc_file <- file.path(work_dir, "adc-dois.rds")
if (file.exists(adc_file)) {
  adc <- readRDS(adc_file)
} else {
  adc <- sub("^doi:", "", read.csv(solr)$id)
  saveRDS(adc, adc_file)
}
length(adc)
```

Delete `adc-dois.rds` to fetch a fresh list.

## Stage 3: The citation graph for all of ADC

Because graph searches are cheap, the third stage runs one over every ADC
DOI. It finds the citations that OpenAlex has linked from articles' reference
lists, and gives a baseline to compare full-text search with in stage 4.

```{r graph}
try(citation_search_openalex(adc, methods = "graph", max_credits = 0))

graph <- citation_search_openalex(adc, methods = "graph",
                                  checkpoint_dir = work_dir, max_credits = 500)
show_status(graph)
nrow(graph)                        # citing article and dataset pairs
length(unique(graph$dataset_id))   # ADC datasets with at least one citing article
```

## Stage 4: Full text on a random sample

Full-text search can be expensive, so the fourth stage runs it on a random
sample of 200 DOIs first. The sample shows what a full run would cost, and
whether full-text search finds enough citations that the graph misses to be
worth that cost.

```{r text}
set.seed(1)
sample_dois <- sample(adc, 200)

try(citation_search_openalex(sample_dois, methods = "text", max_credits = 0))

text <- citation_search_openalex(sample_dois, methods = "text",
                                 checkpoint_dir = work_dir, max_credits = 1500)
show_status(text)
```

The estimate assumes that 5% of the DOIs are cited. If more ADC datasets are
cited than that, full-text search costs more than estimated. Compare the
estimate with what was spent, and with the hit rate in the sample:

```{r text-calibrate}
s <- attr(text, "openalex_status")
c(estimate = s$estimate, spent = s$credits_used,
  hit_rate = length(unique(text$dataset_id)) / length(sample_dois))
```

Then compare the full-text matches with the graph matches for the same
sample:

```{r text-vs-graph}
graph_sample <- graph[scythe:::normalize_doi(graph$dataset_id) %in%
                        scythe:::normalize_doi(sample_dois), ]
text_pairs <- pair(text$article_id, text$dataset_id)
graph_pairs <- pair(graph_sample$article_id, graph_sample$dataset_id)
c(text_only = sum(!text_pairs %in% graph_pairs),
  graph_only = sum(!graph_pairs %in% text_pairs),
  both = sum(text_pairs %in% graph_pairs))
```

`text_only` counts the citations that only full-text search found. Check a
few of them by hand, since full-text matches can include false positives:

```{r text-only}
text[!text_pairs %in% graph_pairs, ]
```

## Stage 5: The full search, in daily installments

The last stage runs both methods over every ADC DOI. Its estimated cost is far
more than a single day's budget, so it runs in installments: it spends credits
until the day's budget is down to its reserve (5% by default; see the
`scythe.openalex.reserve` option) or OpenAlex returns a rate limit error, and
then returns the results found so far.

Run this chunk again each day, with the same `work_dir`, until `complete` is
`TRUE`. The checkpoints skip the batches already done. The file
`openalex-state.json` in `work_dir` records when the rate limit ends, so that
no R session using the same directory sends requests before then.

```{r full, eval = FALSE}
full <- citation_search_openalex(adc, checkpoint_dir = work_dir,
                                 max_credits = Inf, preflight = FALSE)
show_status(full)
saveRDS(full, file.path(work_dir, paste0("full-", Sys.Date(), ".rds")))
```

## Reviewing the results

Besides the citations it returns, each search writes JSON Lines files to
`work_dir` for review. `openalex-matches.jsonl` lists every article match and
which method found it. `openalex-data-relations.jsonl` lists datasets that
cite or mention other datasets. Spot-check both for false positives.
`classify_data_relations(work_dir)` can also label each data relation, using
DataCite, as a version, derivation, composition or citation link; that isn't
needed for the citation counts above.

```{r review}
list.files(work_dir, pattern = "\\.jsonl$")
matches <- jsonlite::stream_in(file(file.path(work_dir, "openalex-matches.jsonl")),
                               verbose = FALSE)
head(matches)
```

## Running this vignette

Building the package doesn't run the searches in this vignette, which only
shows their code. To run stages 1 to 4 and see their output, set the
`SCYTHE_TEST_OPENALEX` environment variable and build the vignette from the
package source directory:

```{r render, eval = FALSE}
Sys.setenv(SCYTHE_TEST_OPENALEX = "true")
rmarkdown::render("vignettes/openalex-arctic-data-center.Rmd")
```

When it runs live, the vignette keeps its logs and checkpoints in
`~/scythe-adc`. Stage 5 never runs when the vignette is built. Run it from the
console.
